newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Kuehbacher sees room for rate cut-spokeswoman.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Kuehbacher sees room for rate cut-spokeswoman.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher said German interest rates, including the 2.50 percent discount rate, could fall further if economic conditions permitted, a spokeswoman said on Thursday.

"There is potentially room for lower interest rates, including the discount rate," the spokeswoman for the regional central bank of Berlin and Brandenburg confirmed Kuehbacher as having told a news agency in an interview conducted on Monday.
Kuehbacher is the president of the state central bank in Berlin and Brandenburg.
The spokeswoman said Kuehbacher had said the central bank's main money market rate, the repo, could fall another 20 basis points from its current three percent level.
But she also added that Kuehbacher had cautioned that no policy move was imminent as the central bank continued to monitor economic developments.
Kuehbacher said additional data was needed before taking another decision but declined to specify what data he had in mind.

Earlier this week, Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke told Reuters Financial Television there may be more room to ease the repo rate if M3 money supply growth, a key policy indicator, continued to slow.
Kuehbacher said he expected M3 money supply growth, standing at 8.6 percent in July, to return to the upper end of the Bundesbank's target corridor of four to seven percent in October or November.

The Bundesbank in late August surprised markets when it sliced a hefty 30 basis points off the repo rate moving it to three percent but leaving the discount rate, the floor for interest rates, at 2.50 percent.
Slower M3 growth, moderate price developments and a slightly firmer mark, which effectively tightened German monetary policy, all helped pave the way for that decision, the Bundesbank explained.

Since then the central bank has on several occasions, and most recently in its September report which was released this morning, said that the easing created clarity on interest rates for the time being.
Speaking about Europe's planned currency union, the spokeswoman confirmed that Kuehbacher urged nations accept a very strict interpretation of the entry criteria laid out in the Maastricht Treaty.

"It is three percent or nothing at all," Kuehbacher was quoted as saying, referring to one of several criteria stating that nations' budget deficits should not exceed three percent of gross domestic product.

The Bundesbank has repeatedly said it favours a very strict interpretation of the entry criteria and has also urged approval of a so-called stability pact, ensuring lasting fiscal austerity once nations have joined the currency union.
Kuehbacher also did not share some policy makers' optimism about Germany's economic recovery, saying "it will be a struggle to reach 1.5 percent growth" next year.
Some policy makers have predicted that German economic growth can reach two to 2.5 percent next year.
